questions.q: What is the single most common cause of SOQL/DML governor-limit failures in real Apex code?
options: Issuing a SOQL query or a DML statement inside a loop, once per iteration
Using too many variables in a single method
Declaring a class without an access modifier
Using Decimal instead of Double for currency fields
questions.explain: Putting a query or DML statement inside a loop means the number of queries/statements scales with the number of records processed, which is exactly what breaches the per-transaction limits at scale.

questions.q: In the fixed pattern, what does `new Map<Id, Account>(accountList)` actually do?
options: It creates an empty Map and ignores accountList entirely
It deletes every Account in accountList
It builds a Map keyed automatically by each Account's Id field, from the records in accountList
It sorts accountList by Name before returning it
questions.explain: Passing a list of sObjects to the Map<Id, SObjectType> constructor builds a map automatically keyed by each record's Id, enabling fast .get() lookups without additional queries.

questions.q: Why might code that updates 5 test records work fine in testing but fail on 300 real records in production?
options: Apex code always behaves differently on weekends
Production orgs have lower governor limits than sandboxes by design
300 records always triggers a different set of governor limits entirely
If a query or DML statement sits inside a loop, the count scales with record volume, and 300 iterations can breach a limit that 5 iterations never approached
questions.explain: The SOQL/DML-in-a-loop anti-pattern scales linearly with record count, so a small test volume can hide a limit breach that only appears once real-world volumes are large enough.

questions.q: What is the recommended fix for code that builds several Task records inside a loop and needs to insert them?
options: Call insert inside the loop immediately after building each Task
Build all the Task records into a List across the loop, then call insert once after the loop ends
Only ever insert one record at a time, since Apex can't insert lists
Use a SOQL for loop instead of DML entirely
questions.explain: Collecting records into a List across the loop and issuing a single DML statement after the loop keeps the DML statement count constant regardless of how many records were built.

questions.q: How does this lesson's fix relate to the bulkification principle from Chapter 3's trigger lessons?
options: It's the same underlying discipline — avoiding per-record queries/DML — generalized from trigger code to any Apex code, since governor limits apply per transaction everywhere
They are unrelated; bulkification only applies inside triggers
Bulkification is about security, while this lesson is only about performance
This lesson's pattern replaces the need for bulkification in triggers
questions.explain: Bulkification in triggers and the query-once/DML-once pattern here are the same principle applied generally: governor limits are enforced per transaction, not per object or line of code, so any Apex code needs this discipline.
